Benefits Signal — candidate digest for the issue of Wednesday, September 2, 2026

Eight candidate developments for review. Review each candidate as it would appear in the newsletter, then the reviewer notes. Record decisions in data/reviews/2026-09-02.json.

1. WATCH · No action yet

Benefits commentary reports that the Medicare Part D demonstration program will end on December 31, 2026

Reported in commentary; legal status not yet confirmed · Stated end date December 31, 2026, date not yet confirmed

Segal reports that a Medicare Part D demonstration program will end earlier than planned, with a stated end date of December 31, 2026, and that the early end affects premiums and retiree health plans.

For a fund that provides retiree prescription drug coverage through a Part D-based arrangement, the question this raises is what the fund pays for that coverage in 2027. The commentary is the only source in the cluster; no agency document confirming the termination or its date has been located, so this is a lead to verify rather than a settled change trustees should act on.

No primary authority supports this item. The termination, its stated December 31, 2026 date, and which Part D arrangements it reaches are all unverified, and that is what holds the item at WATCH. Do not use the date for 2027 budgeting until CMS guidance confirms it.

Read briefing and evidence

  • Who: Multiemployer health and welfare funds that provide retiree prescription drug coverage through a Medicare Part D-based arrangement
  • What: Ask the fund's consultant or carrier whether the fund's retiree prescription drug arrangement relies on the demonstration, and have counsel or the consultant confirm the reported termination and its date against CMS before it is used for 2027 budgeting.
  • By when: No confirmed date. The reported December 31, 2026 end has not been verified against CMS, so the near-term step is confirmation, not a trustee decision. Confirmation should come before the fund sets 2027 retiree coverage and rates.

2. WATCH · No action yet

Groom Law Group reports that the tri-agencies have issued enforcement relief on the HIPAA wellness program full-reward requirement

Reported agency enforcement relief · status not yet confirmed · date not yet confirmed

A Groom Law Group alert dated August 27, 2026 reports that the three agencies that administer the HIPAA wellness program rules have issued enforcement relief concerning the requirement to provide the full reward. The firm describes the background as more than 80 putative class actions alleging that wellness programs charging a premium surcharge for tobacco use violate ERISA, with the central dispute being whether an employer may drop the surcharge going forward once a participant who uses tobacco completes the program's requirement. The excerpt available in the cluster breaks off at that point, so the terms and conditions of the relief are not described here.

For a fund that charges a tobacco-use premium surcharge, relief of this kind would affect how the surcharge is administered and how the program is written up in plan materials. Nothing in the cluster establishes that the relief exists as described, what it covers, how long it lasts, or whether it reaches the pending private lawsuits, which agency enforcement relief ordinarily would not. Trustees should not change surcharge practice on the strength of this item alone.

The relief is reported by a single law firm alert and no agency document was located, so its existence, scope, and duration are unverified. Agency enforcement relief also would not by itself resolve the private class actions the alert describes, so a fund facing surcharge claims should not treat this as a defense until counsel reviews the actual guidance.

Read briefing and evidence

  • Who: Multiemployer health and welfare funds that operate wellness programs with tobacco-use premium surcharges, and the administrators and service providers that run those programs
  • What: Confirm through counsel that the tri-agency relief was actually issued and read its terms before changing how the fund administers any tobacco-use premium surcharge or credits participants who complete the program's alternative.
  • By when: No confirmed date. The relief document has not been located, so there is no deadline to calendar; the follow-up is to find and read it.

Labor Department grants a prohibited-transaction exemption letting a St. Louis carpenters apprenticeship fund sell real property to its affiliated regional council

Granted · Published August 21, 2026 · effective date not yet confirmed

The Employee Benefits Security Administration published a notice granting an individual prohibited-transaction exemption to the Mid-America Carpenters Regional Council Apprentice and Training Fund in St. Louis, Missouri. The exemption allows the fund to sell real property to the Mid-America Carpenters Regional Council; the notice states that without the exemption the sale would be barred by ERISA.

The relief is specific to this applicant and this sale, and imposes nothing on other funds. Its use to trustees elsewhere is as a reminder of the rule it works around: a training trust or welfare fund that sells or transfers its property to the sponsoring union or another party in interest needs exemptive relief, either a class exemption or an individual application to the Department, before the transaction closes.

The notice as supplied does not include the conditions EBSA attached to the relief, an exemption or application number, or any effective date, so it cannot be read as a template for how a comparable sale should be structured.

The notice gives no effective date, no exemption or application number, and none of the conditions attached to the relief. A trustee should not treat the grant as showing that a similar sale would be approved, or on what terms, until the full text with its conditions is obtained.

Read briefing and evidence

  • Who: Multiemployer apprenticeship and training trusts, and multiemployer welfare funds generally, that own real property and are considering a sale or transfer to an affiliated union entity or other party in interest. The relief itself runs only to the Mid-America Carpenters Regional Council Apprentice and Training Fund.
  • What: If the fund is considering selling or transferring fund-owned property to the sponsoring union, an affiliated council, or a contributing employer association, have counsel confirm before closing whether a class exemption applies or an individual exemption must be applied for. Otherwise, note the grant as background.
  • By when: No deadline. The notice imposes no obligation on other funds; act only if a sale or transfer of fund property to a party in interest is under discussion, in which case relief must be settled before closing.

    • Prohibited Transactions & Expense Reasonableness: The notice is the exemptive relief that makes an otherwise prohibited sale of plan property to a party in interest permissible, which is the mechanism trustees must use for such dealings.
    • Loyalty & Exclusive Benefit: The buyer is the sponsoring regional council, so the grant addresses a transaction in which trustees must show the sale serves the fund and its participants rather than the affiliated union.
  • Verification: partially_confirmed (status confirmed, dates partially_confirmed, posture partially_confirmed) — primary
    This cluster has no commentary documents — the Federal Register notice is the only member — so there are no third-party assertions to test. What follows records only what the primary document itself states and what it leaves unstated. What the primary states: it is a "Federal Register — Labor Department, Employee Benefits Security Administration" item dated 2026-08-21, typed "Notice," with document_number "2026-17144," captioned "Exemption for Certain Prohibited Transactions Involving Mid-America Carpenters Regional Council Apprentice and Training Fund (the Fund or Applicant) Located in St. Louis, Missouri." The body reads: "This exemption permits the sale by the Fund of real property to the Mid-America Carpenters Regional Council (the Sale). Without this exemption, the Sale would be prohibited by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA)." Status — confirmed as internally consistent: the caption ("Exemption for...") and the operative sentence ("This exemption permits...") both describe a granted individual prohibited-transaction exemption, in the present tense, not a notice of proposed exemption and not a request for comment. The document type field "Notice" is consistent with how EBSA publishes granted exemptions. Nothing in the supplied text contradicts anything else in it. Dates — only one date is present. The publication date is given as "2026-08-21." The document as supplied states no effective date, no retroactive or prospective applicability date for the Sale, no comment deadline (consistent with a grant rather than a proposal), and no date by which the Sale must be completed. Anyone describing when this exemption takes effect, or whether relief runs retroactively, would be going beyond the primary document. Recorded as partially confirmed because the publication date is stated while every operative date is absent. Posture — the agency and document type are stated (EBSA; "Notice"), and the document is on its face the exemption grant its caption describes, so the action matches the caption. But the primary supplies no exemption number (no "PTE 2026-__"), no application or docket number (no "D-" number identifying the Applicant's file), no citation to a prior notice of proposed exemption, and no Federal Register volume or page. The only identifier available is document_number "2026-17144." Recorded as partially confirmed on that basis. The primary document also does not state: the address or description of the real property, the sale price or how it was determined, the identity or role of any independent fiduciary or qualified appraiser, the conditions attached to the relief, whether the Council is a party in interest by reason of a specific ERISA section, or any comment history. None of that should be supplied from background knowledge of how EBSA exemptions are ordinarily structured. Overall result is partially confirmed: status is confirmed on the document's own terms, while dates and posture are each only partially supported by the fields supplied.

Law-firm commentary reports DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2026-01 on EBSA's approach to ERISA investigation and enforcement

Sub-regulatory guidance as described by commentary · date not yet confirmed

A Trucker Huss Benefits Report post states that the Department of Labor issued Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2026-01 on April 14, 2026, giving guidance on how the Employee Benefits Security Administration approaches the investigation and enforcement of ERISA. The post says the bulletin is directed principally to EBSA staff but draws practical takeaways for plan sponsors and other fiduciaries.

A field assistance bulletin instructs agency investigators rather than imposing new obligations on plans, so the significance for a fund lies in what it signals about how an EBSA investigation would be conducted and what an investigator would ask for. The specific takeaways are not available to us: the commentary text in the cluster stops after the opening description.

No primary authority was located for this item. The bulletin's existence, number, date, and content have not been checked against the Department, and the briefing should not be treated as an account of what the bulletin actually says.

The bulletin itself was not located and the commentary excerpt is truncated before its practical takeaways, so what FAB 2026-01 tells investigators is unknown. Trustees should treat this as a prompt to obtain the source document, not as guidance to act on.

Read briefing and evidence

  • Who: Multiemployer health and welfare plans and their trustees, as ERISA plan fiduciaries subject to EBSA investigation; the commentary describes the bulletin as directed principally to EBSA staff.
  • What: Ask counsel to obtain the text of FAB 2026-01 from the Department and determine whether EBSA's stated investigation and enforcement approach calls for any change in how the fund documents its fiduciary decisions and responds to information requests. Do not act on the commentary summary alone.
  • By when: No confirmed date and no deadline reported. The April 14, 2026 issuance date comes only from the commentary and has not been verified, so the work to do first is locating the bulletin itself rather than meeting a deadline.

Ninth Circuit files a published opinion in Liu v. Kaiser Permanente Employees Pension Plan, No. 24-4303

Decided · Published opinion filed August 31, 2026

The Ninth Circuit filed a published opinion on August 31, 2026 in Liu v. Kaiser Permanente Employees Pension Plan for the Permanente Medical Group, Inc., No. 24-4303, an appeal from the Northern District of California, No. 3:23-cv-03109-AMO. The plaintiff, Sherry Yali Liu, is the appellant; the plan and a Kaiser Foundation entity are the appellees.

The text captured in the cluster ends in the caption. It supplies no disposition, no panel, no statement of the claims, and no legal holding, and it says nothing about whether the mandate has issued or whether rehearing has been sought. The only fact the record establishes beyond the caption is that the opinion is published, which means it will be citable precedent in this circuit once its content is known.

For a fund, the practical consequence today is limited to retrieval and review. Because the substance is not in the record, the briefing cannot say whether the decision bears on plan administration, claims handling, or fiduciary standards, and no fund practice should be changed on the strength of this entry alone.

The disposition and the legal issue are unknown, and post-decision status (mandate, rehearing, amendment) is unstated. That is what holds this at WATCH: the same entry could warrant attorney review immediately if the opinion turns out to address ERISA standards that reach jointly administered funds.

Read briefing and evidence

  • Who: Not yet determinable. The caption names a single-employer pension plan and its sponsor, not a multiemployer welfare or training fund; whether the decision reaches jointly administered funds in the Ninth Circuit depends on a holding the record does not supply.
  • What: Have counsel pull the full slip opinion (No. 24-4303) and read the disposition before treating this case as relevant to the fund; nothing in the record now supports a change to fund practice.
  • By when: No confirmed deadline. The opinion was filed August 31, 2026; the record states no mandate date and no rehearing deadline, so the only time-sensitive step is retrieving the full text.

Treasury and IRS propose rules on employer contributions to Trump accounts and on nondiscrimination for dependent care assistance programs

Proposed, status not yet confirmed · Comment deadline date not yet confirmed

Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service have published a proposal that would set out guidance on employer contributions to Trump accounts, including the nondiscrimination rules that would apply to those contributions, and would also address the nondiscrimination rules for dependent care assistance programs. The notice includes a public hearing.

By its own description, the proposal reaches employers that maintain either kind of program and the employees who participate in them. Nothing in the cluster document places an obligation on a jointly administered fund as such, so the immediate question for a fund is whether it or its contributing employers maintain a dependent care assistance program that the nondiscrimination provisions would touch.

Verification did not run on this item. The status, the comment close date, and the procedural posture are all unconfirmed, so the notice should be checked directly before any deadline is calendared or any comment decision is made.

Verification failed on this item, so the proposed status, the comment close date, and the hearing date are all unconfirmed. The stated comment deadline is what would make this time-sensitive; until someone confirms it against the Federal Register entry, the reader should treat the timing as unknown rather than assume a short window has been missed.

Read briefing and evidence

  • Who: Employers that maintain a dependent care assistance program or a Trump account contribution program, and employees participating in those programs. No fund-level obligation is identified in the cluster document.
  • What: Confirm whether the fund or its contributing employers maintain a dependent care assistance program that the nondiscrimination provisions would reach, and confirm the comment deadline and current status directly against the Federal Register entry before treating this as time-sensitive.
  • By when: No confirmed date. The notice states a comment deadline, but verification did not run, so there is nothing confirmed to calendar. Confirm the entry first; if the deadline is verified, it falls within weeks, so confirmation should not be deferred.
